title: The Two Gentlemen of Verona
description: Shakespeare's early romantic comedy of friendship and betrayal: Valentine and Proteus, the 'two gentlemen' of Verona, both fall in love with Silvia; Proteus betrays his friend and his own beloved Julia, and the play moves through disguise, forest outlawry, and attempted rape to a reconciliation whose abruptness has troubled audiences ever since.
plot_or_argument: Proteus, sent to Milan, falls in love with Valentine's Silvia and betrays him to the Duke; Valentine joins the outlaws, Silvia flees to the forest, and Proteus's assault on her is stopped by Valentine's intervention, leading to the double reconciliation and the play's famously compressed ending.
narrative_structure: Five acts of alternating Milan and forest scenes, built on the paired lovers plot with the comic servants Speed and Launce (and his dog Crab) as counterpoint.
principal_characters: Valentine; Proteus; Silvia; Julia; the Duke of Milan; Launce; Speed; Crab the dog
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse and prose, with songs; among Shakespeare's earliest surviving verse.
historical_context: An early play, probably written about 1590–91 from the Spanish romance Diana Enamorada (via its French and English versions); not printed until the 1623 First Folio.
literary_significance: The first of Shakespeare's romantic comedies and the seedbed of themes — friendship versus love, the heroine in disguise, the green world — he would develop for a decade.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: The Taming of the Shrew
description: Shakespeare's farcical comedy of courtship and domestication: the fortune-hunter Petruchio 'tames' the headstrong Katherine of Padua by a regime of contradiction and deprivation, while her sister Bianca is courted by a crowd of disguised suitors — all framed by the Induction, in which the drunken tinker Christopher Sly is tricked into believing himself a lord for whom the play is performed.
plot_or_argument: Sly is gulled into watching a play: Lucentio disguises himself to woo Bianca, his servant Tranio impersonates him, and Petruchio marries Katherine and breaks her will — or teaches her the game — until she delivers the play's closing speech on wives' obedience, its irony a matter of perennial dispute.
narrative_structure: An Induction framing a two-plot comedy (the Bianca courtship intrigue and the Petruchio–Kate duel), in the manner of Italian commedia-derived farce.
principal_characters: Christopher Sly; Petruchio; Katherine; Bianca; Lucentio; Tranio; Baptista Minola; Grumio; Hortensio; Gremio
meter_and_prosody: Mostly prose and doggerel in the farcical scenes, with blank verse for the courtship of Kate and Petruchio.
historical_context: Written about 1590–92, in dialogue with the anonymous play The Taming of a Shrew (1594); its debate over wifely subjection has made it the most contested of the comedies in modern performance and criticism.
literary_significance: Shakespeare's most durable farce, endlessly revived and argued over — a test case for every generation's view of marriage, gender, and power.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the relation to the anonymous A Shrew remains debated.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: The Comedy of Errors
description: Shakespeare's shortest play and his only pure farce, built on Plautus's Menaechmi: twin masters and twin servants, both pairs named Antipholus and Dromio, are separated by shipwreck and reunited by coincidence in Ephesus, where the confusions of mistaken identity multiply until the family is restored in the recognition scene before the Abbess.
plot_or_argument: Antipholus of Syracuse and his servant Dromio arrive in Ephesus, where their long-lost twins live; the day becomes a cascade of wrong beatings, wrong dinners, and wrong arrests, until the Duke's judgment and the Abbess's revelation untangle the knots and reunite husband, wife, and sons.
narrative_structure: A single-day, single-city action — the closest Shakespeare came to the classical unities — with the errors compounded scene by scene to the recognition finale.
principal_characters: Antipholus of Syracuse; Antipholus of Ephesus; Dromio of Syracuse; Dromio of Ephesus; Adriana; Luciana; Egeon; the Abbess (Emilia); the Duke
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse with prose for the servants' comedy; the play includes the verse 'discourse' scene between Antipholus of Syracuse and Luciana.
historical_context: Probably written for Gray's Inn's Christmas revels of 1594; the frame of Egeon's doom under Ephesian law darkens the farce with the threat of execution.
literary_significance: The most technically perfect of the early comedies and Shakespeare's demonstration that classical comedy could be outdone in English.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Love's Labour's Lost
description: Shakespeare's most verbally extravagant comedy: the King of Navarre and his three lords swear a three-year vow of study, fasting, and no women — a vow broken at once by the arrival of the Princess of France and her ladies, whose wit outmatches the men's until the play's astonishing turn: news of the Princess's father's death converts the comedy into a year of penance and a set of unfinished songs.
plot_or_argument: The lords woo the ladies in disguise and are exposed; the pedants Holofernes and Nathaniel stage the pageant of the Nine Worthies and are mocked; and just as the marriages are to be concluded, Marcade enters with the news of the French king's death, and the ladies impose their year-long conditions on the suitors.
narrative_structure: A plotless, tournament-like comedy of wit built on symmetrical scenes of courtship, masque, and pageant, ending in the deliberately anti-comic 'dialogue' of Spring and Winter songs.
principal_characters: Ferdinand, King of Navarre; Berowne; Longaville; Dumaine; the Princess of France; Rosaline; Maria; Katherine; Boyet; Don Armado; Holofernes; Nathaniel; Costard; Jaquenetta; Moth
meter_and_prosody: The highest proportion of rhyme in Shakespeare, with sonnets, songs, and the prose of the pedants' Latinity.
historical_context: Written about 1594–95 amid the French succession crisis and the Euphuistic wordplay fashion it both satirizes and surpasses; first printed in quarto, 1598.
literary_significance: The summit of Elizabethan verbal comedy and the play in which Shakespeare's lyric genius first runs free.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1598; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
description: Shakespeare's fairy comedy of lovers, artisans, and the dream-wood: four Athenian lovers flee into the forest, the fairy king and queen quarrel over an Indian boy, Puck's love-juice scrambles every affection, and the 'rude mechanicals' rehearse the tragedy of Pyramus and Thisbe — the whole resolved at dawn into Theseus's wedding feast and the play-within-the-play.
plot_or_argument: Hermia must marry Demetrius or die; she flees with Lysander, pursued by Demetrius and Helena; Oberon's magic makes both men love Helena; Titania, enchanted, dotes on Bottom the weaver in his ass's head; all is set right by dawn, and the mechanicals' catastrophic performance of 'Pyramus and Thisbe' crowns the triple wedding.
narrative_structure: Four interwoven plots — court, lovers, fairies, artisans — braided through the night and united in the final act's play-within-the-play.
principal_characters: Theseus; Hippolyta; Lysander; Demetrius; Hermia; Helena; Oberon; Titania; Puck (Robin Goodfellow); Nick Bottom; Peter Quince; Francis Flute; Egeus
meter_and_prosody: Lyric blank verse for the lovers and fairies, prose for the mechanicals, with the songs and charms of the fairy scenes.
historical_context: Probably written for an aristocratic wedding about 1595–96; its 'rude mechanicals' satirize the artisan theatre culture of Elizabethan London.
literary_significance: The most perfect English comedy of the supernatural, and the play through which most of the world first meets Shakespeare.
bibliographical_notes: Quartos 1600, 1619; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: The Merchant of Venice
description: Shakespeare's comedy of credit, bonds, and mercy: the merchant Antonio pledges a pound of his own flesh to the Jewish moneylender Shylock to fund his friend Bassanio's courtship of the heiress Portia, who — disguised as a lawyer — saves Antonio in the trial scene and turns the bond against its maker.
plot_or_argument: Bassanio wins Portia by choosing the lead casket; Shylock, his daughter Jessica fled with a Christian and his bond forfeited, claims his pound of flesh; Portia's legal trap — the bond allows flesh but not blood — defeats him, and the play ends with the ring trick and the news of Antonio's restored argosies, leaving Shylock's forced conversion and the play's anti-Semitism to shadow the comedy.
narrative_structure: Interlaced Venice and Belmont plots — the bond and the caskets — joined at the trial, with the Jessica–Lorenzo elopement and the ring episode as connecting tissue.
principal_characters: Antonio; Shylock; Bassanio; Portia; Jessica; Lorenzo; Nerissa; Gratiano; the Duke of Venice; Tubal; Launcelot Gobbo
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse for the trial and courtship, prose for the Venetian streets, with the lyric interludes of 'Tell me where is fancy bred'.
historical_context: Written about 1596–97, in the aftermath of the Lopez affair and against the background of the Venetian Ghetto; its Jew is both the period's stock villain and its most human outsider.
literary_significance: One of the most performed and most contested plays in the canon — the 'Hath not a Jew eyes?' speech and the quality-of-mercy plea are cornerstones of world drama.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1600; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: The Merry Wives of Windsor
description: Shakespeare's only citizen comedy, traditionally said to have been written because Elizabeth I wished to see Falstaff in love: the fat knight courts the wives Mistress Ford and Mistress Page, who turn the tables on him through the buck-basket, the disguise of the fat woman of Brentford, and the final horns of Herne the Hunter in Windsor Forest.
plot_or_argument: Falstaff sends identical love letters to two wives, who conspire to humiliate him; Ford's jealousy supplies a second plot of disguise and misprision; and the play resolves in the midnight masque of the fairies, where Falstaff is pinched and the eloping Anne Page marries the suitor of her choice against her parents' plots.
narrative_structure: A three-humiliation comic structure (basket, beating, forest masque) interwoven with the Anne Page marriage intrigue and the Latin lesson of Sir Hugh Evans and William.
principal_characters: Sir John Falstaff; Mistress Ford; Mistress Page; Ford; Page; Anne Page; Fenton; Slender; Doctor Caius; Sir Hugh Evans; Mistress Quickly; Pistol; Nym; the Host
meter_and_prosody: Over ninety percent prose — the most prosaic of Shakespeare's plays — with the fairy rhymes of the final scene.
historical_context: Dated about 1597, possibly for a Garter feast at Windsor; it transplants Falstaff from the history plays into contemporary Windsor life.
literary_significance: Shakespeare's only comedy of his own England and time — the ancestor of the English sitcom and the later operatic masterpieces it inspired.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1602 (bad); First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Much Ado About Nothing
description: Shakespeare's comedy of wit and slander: the 'merry war' of Beatrice and Benedick is tricked into love by their friends, while the villain Don John's plot makes Claudio believe his bride Hero unfaithful — a lie that kills her (apparently) at the altar, until the watch's comic detective work exposes the plot and Hero returns from the dead.
plot_or_argument: Don Pedro's court at Messina: Claudio and Hero are betrothed; Beatrice and Benedick are gulled into confessing love by overheard conversations; Don John stages the scene of Hero's infidelity with Margaret; Hero is denounced and shammed dead; Dogberry and the Watch stumble on the truth, and the double wedding concludes the play.
narrative_structure: Twin plots of courtship — the gulling of Beatrice and Benedick, and the destruction and restoration of Hero — joined by the watch's comic inquest.
principal_characters: Beatrice; Benedick; Claudio; Hero; Don Pedro; Don John; Leonato; Dogberry; Verges; Margaret; Borachio; Conrade; Friar Francis
meter_and_prosody: Prose for the wit-combats, blank verse for the romantic crises, with the songs of Balthasar.
historical_context: Written about 1598–99 from Bandello via Ariosto; printed in quarto, 1600; among the first plays staged after the reopening of the theatres under James I.
literary_significance: The model of the comedy of wit, whose sparring lovers founded a tradition running through Restoration comedy to the screwball film.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1600; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: As You Like It
description: Shakespeare's pastoral comedy, adapted from Thomas Lodge's Rosalynde: Duke Senior, exiled to the Forest of Arden, is joined by his daughter Rosalind (disguised as the boy Ganymede), her cousin Celia, the clown Touchstone, and eventually the melancholy Jaques and the reformed usurper — while Orlando's love-verses to Rosalind hang on every tree.
plot_or_argument: Orlando, robbed of his birthright, flees to Arden; Rosalind, banished, tutors him in love while disguised as Ganymede; the usurping Duke is converted on the forest's edge; and the play ends with four weddings and the god Hymen's masque, followed by Rosalind's epilogue.
narrative_structure: A movement from court to forest and back, built on the contrast of the two worlds and on the play's chain of love-dialogues, with the 'Seven Ages of Man' speech and the songs of Amiens as set pieces.
principal_characters: Rosalind; Orlando; Celia; Touchstone; Jaques; Duke Senior; Duke Frederick; Oliver; Adam; Silvius; Phebe; Audrey; William; Corin; Charles the wrestler
meter_and_prosody: Alternating prose and blank verse — Rosalind's prose wit against Orlando's verses — with the songs 'Under the greenwood tree' and 'It was a lover and his lass'.
historical_context: Written 1599, the year of the Globe's opening, from Lodge's Rosalynde (1590); the forest reimagines the Ardennes through Warwickshire memory.
literary_significance: The definitive English pastoral comedy and the vehicle of Shakespeare's greatest comic heroine.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Twelfth Night
alternative_titles: Twelfth Night, or What You Will
description: Shakespeare's comedy of disguise and desire: Viola, shipwrecked in Illyria, serves Duke Orsino disguised as the boy Cesario and carries his love-suit to Olivia — who falls in love with Cesario — while the Puritan steward Malvolio is gulled into yellow stockings by the forged letter, and the revels of Sir Toby and the clown roll on to the reunion of the twins.
plot_or_argument: Orsino loves Olivia; Olivia loves Cesario (Viola); Viola loves Orsino; the triangle dissolves when Sebastian, Viola's twin, appears and marries Olivia; Malvolio's humiliation darkens the last scene with his promise of revenge — 'I'll be revenged on the whole pack of you'.
narrative_structure: Two households — Orsino's and Olivia's — with the sub-plot of Sir Toby, Sir Andrew, Maria, and Feste against Malvolio, all resolved by the twins' reunion.
principal_characters: Viola (Cesario); Orsino; Olivia; Sebastian; Malvolio; Sir Toby Belch; Sir Andrew Aguecheek; Maria; Feste; Antonio; Fabian
meter_and_prosody: A flexible mix of blank verse, prose, and song, with Feste's 'Come away, come away, death' and the closing rain-song.
historical_context: Performed 1601–02 (the Middle Temple performance of 2 February 1602 is recorded); the title marks the Feast of Epiphany and the licence of holiday misrule.
literary_significance: The crowning achievement of Shakespearean comedy — the subtlest study of erotic fluidity before modern drama — and the seed of a thousand later plots.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: All's Well That Ends Well
description: Shakespeare's 'problem comedy' from Boccaccio: Helena, the physician's daughter, cures the King of France and claims as her reward the reluctant Bertram, who flees to the wars of Italy — forcing Helena to win him by the bed-trick: taking Diana's place in the dark to fulfil his impossible conditions (his ring and his child), and exposing him at the play's end.
plot_or_argument: Helena heals the King, chooses Bertram, is rejected and abandoned; in Florence she substitutes herself for Diana in Bertram's bed and secures ring and child; the final scene unravels Bertram's lies until Helena appears with both proofs and his conversion is wrung from him.
narrative_structure: A fairy-tale plot (the healing of the king, the impossible tasks) crossed with the bed-trick of Renaissance novella, framed by the choric commentaries of the Countess, Lafew, and Parolles.
principal_characters: Helena; Bertram; the Countess of Rousillon; the King of France; Parolles; Lafew; Diana; the Widow; the two French lords (the Dumaine brothers)
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse with prose for the exposure of Parolles; the style is spare and riddling, matching the play's moral knot.
historical_context: Dated about 1604–05, in the same phase as Measure for Measure; its tone reflects the Jacobean darkening of Shakespeare's comedy.
literary_significance: The most disquieting of the comedies — a study of merit against rank, and of a woman's will — that has found its audience only in the modern era.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Measure for Measure
description: Shakespeare's great comedy of justice and mercy: the Duke of Vienna, disguised as a friar, leaves the puritanical Angelo to enforce the city's neglected laws; Angelo condemns Claudio to death for fornication, then offers to spare him if his sister Isabella will yield her virginity — a bargain exposed in the final judgment scene, where the Duke returns to measure all by their own measure.
plot_or_argument: Angelo revives the death penalty for lechery; Claudio's sister Isabella pleads for him; Angelo's blackmail and the bed-trick with the jilted Mariana preserve Isabella and expose Angelo; the Duke's staged return conducts the play's long trial-and-pardon finale, ending with his abrupt proposal to Isabella.
narrative_structure: A legal fable on the title's biblical text, built on the Duke's disguised supervision and resolved in the massed judgment scene of Act 5.
principal_characters: Duke Vincentio; Angelo; Isabella; Claudio; Mariana; Lucio; Escalus; Pompey; Mistress Overdone; Elbow; the Provost; Barnardine
meter_and_prosody: A grave, economical blank verse, with the prose of the Vienna underworld (Pompey, Lucio) as corrosive chorus.
historical_context: Performed at court, 26 December 1604; the play's Vienna shadows Jacobean London's anxieties over plague, puritanism, and the royal exercise of mercy.
literary_significance: Shakespeare's deepest study of law, sex, and power — a play that has grown darker and more central with every century.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; minor passages possibly revised by Middleton.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Troilus and Cressida
description: Shakespeare's bitter anatomy of the Trojan War: the lovers Troilus and Cressida are separated by her exchange to the Greeks, and her infidelity with Diomedes poisons their romance, while the Greek camp degenerates into a satire of its own heroes — Achilles sulking, Ajax a blockhead, and the cynical Thersites commentating on the whole — and Hector's chivalry dies under Achilles' Myrmidons.
plot_or_argument: The war stalls; Cressida is traded for a Trojan prisoner and betrays Troilus with Diomedes before his eyes; the debate over Helen, Ulysses' speech on degree, the gulling of Ajax, and the duel of Hector and Ajax fill the middle acts; the play ends with Hector's murder and Pandarus's epilogue bequeathing the audience his diseases.
narrative_structure: A double plot — the love story and the war council — that refuses tragic or comic closure, ending in anti-climax and epilogue.
principal_characters: Troilus; Cressida; Pandarus; Hector; Achilles; Ulysses; Agamemnon; Nestor; Ajax; Diomedes; Thersites; Helen; Priam; Cassandra
meter_and_prosody: A harsh, debate-driven verse, with Thersites' prose invective as the play's running commentary.
historical_context: Written about 1602, in the wake of the 'war of the theatres' and Essex's fall; printed in 1609 with an epistle hailing it as a play never clapper-clawed by the vulgar.
literary_significance: The great Elizabethan debunking of the heroic ideal — the play in which the Renaissance turned its scepticism on its own founding myth.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1609; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Henry VI, Part 1
alternative_titles: The First Part of Henry the Sixth
description: The first play of Shakespeare's earliest tetralogy, probably written in collaboration: the loss of France, the rise and burning of Joan la Pucelle (Joan of Arc), the quarrels of Gloucester and Winchester, and the white rose and the red plucked in the Temple Garden that plant the Wars of the Roses.
plot_or_argument: Henry V's funeral opens the play; the French recover their towns through Joan's victories; Talbot, the English Achilles, dies at Bordeaux; the factions of York and Lancaster form in England; and the play ends with Suffolk's capture of Margaret of Anjou as Henry's bride — and his own instrument.
narrative_structure: An episodic chronicle alternating English and French scenes, unified by Talbot's tragedy and the growth of the court factions.
principal_characters: King Henry VI; Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester; the Bishop of Winchester; Richard, Duke of York; the Earl of Warwick; Talbot; Joan la Pucelle; Charles the Dauphin; the Duke of Suffolk; Margaret of Anjou; Edmund Mortimer
meter_and_prosody: Early blank verse, often stiff and end-stopped, with the play's documentary sweep compensating for its poetic unevenness.
historical_context: The Talbot scenes were celebrated by Nashe in 1592; the play is the first in the sequence that runs through Richard III.
literary_significance: The foundation of the English history-play cycle, and the apprenticeship of its greatest master.
attribution_notes: Generally regarded as collaborative (the shares of Nashe and others are debated); assigned to Shakespeare by the Folio.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Henry VI, Part 2
alternative_titles: The First Part of the Contention
The Contention of the Two Famous Houses of York and Lancaster
description: The second play of the tetralogy: the fall of Duke Humphrey of Gloucester, the rebellion of Jack Cade, and the rise of Richard, Duke of York, through the disintegration of Henry VI's England toward the first battle of St Albans.
plot_or_argument: The court faction destroys Gloucester; York exploits the Cade rebellion to test his claim; the play's great set pieces — Gloucester's murder, the miracle at St Albans, Cade's insurrection — carry England from anarchy to open war, with Margaret and Suffolk's fall along the way.
narrative_structure: A chronicle of successive falls (Gloucester, Suffolk, Cade) leading to York's armed claim, in the de casibus pattern of the Mirror for Magistrates.
principal_characters: King Henry VI; Queen Margaret; Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester; Eleanor Cobham; the Duke of Suffolk; the Duke of York; Jack Cade; the Earl of Warwick; the Cardinal (Beaufort); Lord Say; Dick the butcher
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse growing more assured, with the prose of the Cade scenes as the first great crowd-comedy in English drama.
historical_context: The Cade rebellion scenes dramatize the 1450 rising through Elizabethan anxieties about the commons; printed in 1594 as The First Part of the Contention.
literary_significance: The first English play to put the whole commonwealth — commons, court, and crown — on stage together.
attribution_notes: Possibly collaborative with Marlowe or Nashe in debated shares; the Folio canon is followed here.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1594; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Henry VI, Part 3
alternative_titles: The True Tragedy of Richard Duke of York
description: The third play of the tetralogy: the Wars of the Roses in full blood — York's death on the molehill at Wakefield, Margaret's taunting of him with the paper crown, the slaughter of young Rutland, and the rise of Richard of Gloucester through the battles of Towton, Barnet, and Tewkesbury to his soliloquized ambitions at the play's end.
plot_or_argument: York breaks his oath and claims the crown; the wars swing between Lancaster and York; Edward IV wins the throne and marries Elizabeth Woodville; Warwick changes sides and dies at Barnet; and Richard murders Henry VI in the Tower, then turns to the audience to announce his design on the crown.
narrative_structure: A rapid battle-chronicle built on reversals of fortune, with Richard's emergence as the play's climactic revelation.
principal_characters: King Henry VI; Queen Margaret; Richard, Duke of York; Edward IV; George, Duke of Clarence; Richard, Duke of Gloucester; the Earl of Warwick; Lady Grey (Elizabeth Woodville); the Duke of Exeter; Rutland; Clifford
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of mounting power, culminating in Richard's first great soliloquy.
historical_context: Written about 1590–91, the play's cycles of revenge answered the Senecan fashion while its national matter spoke to the post-Armada moment.
literary_significance: The bridge from the Henry VI plays to Richard III — and the first sketch of Shakespeare's greatest villain.
attribution_notes: Possibly collaborative in debated shares; the Folio canon is followed here.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto (octavo), 1595, as The True Tragedy of Richard Duke of York; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Richard III
alternative_titles: The Tragedy of King Richard the Third
description: Shakespeare's first great tragedy, completing the first tetralogy: Richard, Duke of Gloucester, murders his way to the crown through his brothers, his nephews (the Princes in the Tower), and his allies, seducing and discarding Lady Anne along the way, until the ghosts of his victims curse him at Bosworth and Richmond's victory ends the Wars of the Roses and plants the Tudor line.
plot_or_argument: Richard announces his villainy in the opening soliloquy, eliminates Clarence, Hastings, Buckingham, Rivers, and the young princes, weds Anne and then plans her death; at Bosworth the procession of ghosts damns him and blesses Richmond, who slays him and marries Elizabeth of York.
narrative_structure: A Senecan revenge-cum-chronicle play driven by Richard's direct address — the audience as confidant — and crowned by the symmetrical dream of ghosts.
principal_characters: Richard, Duke of Gloucester (Richard III); the Duke of Buckingham; Lady Anne; Queen Elizabeth; Queen Margaret; the Duke of Clarence; Lord Hastings; King Edward IV; the Duchess of York; Henry, Earl of Richmond; the two young Princes
meter_and_prosody: A verse of rhetorical virtuosity — Richard's soliloquies are among the most quoted in the canon — with the stichomythia of the wooing scene.
historical_context: Written about 1592–93 from More's History of King Richard III via the chronicles of Hall and Holinshed; the Tudor myth of Richard's monstrosity serves the founding ideology of the Elizabethan state.
literary_significance: The first fully achieved Shakespearean tragedy of character, and the role that has defined the tragic actor from Burbage to Olivier.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1597; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: King John
alternative_titles: The Life and Death of King John
description: Shakespeare's stand-alone history play of the Angevin crisis: King John's disputed title, the Bastard Faulconbridge's satirical commentary, the struggle with the papal legate Pandulph, and the play's terrible centre — the blinding of the boy Arthur and the grief of his mother Constance — ending in John's poisoning at Swinstead and the Bastard's closing appeal to England's unity.
plot_or_argument: John defies Rome, battles France, captures Arthur, and orders his death; Hubert cannot blind the boy, but Arthur dies in his leap from the walls; the French invasion, the defection of the nobles, and John's poisoning follow, until the Bastard's loyalty and the Dauphin's withdrawal restore the kingdom.
narrative_structure: An episodic chronicle held together by the Bastard's choric commentary and by the Arthur tragedy at its centre.
principal_characters: King John; the Bastard (Philip Faulconbridge); Queen Elinor; Constance; Prince Arthur; Hubert; Cardinal Pandulph; King Philip of France; Lewis the Dauphin; Salisbury; Pembroke
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of strong rhetorical sweep, with Constance's grief and the Bastard's 'commodity' soliloquy as the peaks.
historical_context: Probably written 1595–96 in the anxious interval over the succession; its resistance to papal and foreign power spoke to Reformation England.
literary_significance: Shakespeare's boldest experiment in the history genre — a play without heroes, held together by the Bastard's irony and England's idea of itself.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Richard II
alternative_titles: The Tragedy of King Richard the Second
description: Shakespeare's lyrical tragedy of deposition, opening the second tetralogy: Richard's misgovernment, the quarrel of Bolingbroke and Mowbray, and the king's fall from the throne of England — the first English history play written entirely in verse, culminating in Richard's murder at Pomfret and the new king's guilt.
plot_or_argument: Richard banishes Bolingbroke and seizes his inheritance on Gaunt's death; Bolingbroke returns to claim his own, and the king's support melts away; in the deposition scene Richard unkings himself before Parliament; the plot of Aumerle is discovered, and Exton, reading Henry's wish, kills Richard in prison.
narrative_structure: A five-act fall of princes, symmetrical in its structure of deposition, prophecy, and fulfilment, with the garden scene as the play's emblem of the commonwealth.
principal_characters: King Richard II; Henry Bolingbroke; John of Gaunt; the Duke of York; the Duke of Aumerle; Thomas Mowbray; the Queen; Northumberland; the Bishop of Carlisle; Exton; the Gardener
meter_and_prosody: Entirely in verse, much of it rhymed — Richard's elegiac lyricism is the play's signature music.
historical_context: Written 1595 and printed 1597; the deposition scene was omitted from the early quartos for political reasons, and the play was notoriously performed on the eve of Essex's rising in 1601.
literary_significance: The great English meditation on kingship, legitimacy, and the theatre of power — the seed of the Henriad that follows.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1597; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Henry IV, Part 1
alternative_titles: The First Part of Henry the Fourth
description: The first play of the Henriad proper: Prince Hal's education between the tavern of Falstaff and the field of Shrewsbury, where he kills the rebel Hotspur and redeems his reputation — the comedy of Eastcheap and the tragedy of the Percys joined in the greatest of the English history plays.
plot_or_argument: Hotspur and the Percys rebel against the king they helped make; Hal plays truant with Falstaff until the crisis calls him to arms; at Shrewsbury he saves his father, kills Hotspur, and leaves Falstaff to counterfeit death and claim the honour — a claim the prince allows, 'for my part, if a lie may do thee grace, I'll gild it with the happiest terms I have'.
narrative_structure: A double plot of court/camp and tavern braided by Hal's movement between the two worlds, with the Gadshill robbery as hinge and the battle as convergence.
principal_characters: Prince Hal (Henry, Prince of Wales); Sir John Falstaff; King Henry IV; Hotspur (Henry Percy); the Earl of Worcester; the Earl of Northumberland; Owen Glendower; the Earl of Douglas; Poins; Bardolph; Mistress Quickly; Lady Percy
meter_and_prosody: The fullest range of Shakespeare's early style: Hotspur's verse, Falstaff's prose, Hal's movement between them, and Glendower's Welsh lyricism.
historical_context: Written about 1596–97 from Holinshed and the anonymous Famous Victories of Henry V; Oldcastle's name was changed to Falstaff after protest from the Cobham family.
literary_significance: Contains Shakespeare's greatest comic creation in Falstaff, and his profoundest study of a prince's education in power.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1598; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Henry IV, Part 2
alternative_titles: The Second Part of Henry the Fourth
description: The darker sequel: rebellion flickers out at Gaultree Forest, the king sickens under the weight of his usurped crown, Falstaff conscripts the rag-tag army of Gloucestershire and runs up his tavern score, and the play ends with the new king's public rejection of his old companion — 'I know thee not, old man' — and Falstaff's ruin.
plot_or_argument: Northumberland's rebellion collapses; Prince John tricks the rebels into disbanding; the dying king and Hal are reconciled; Henry V's coronation is followed by the rejection of Falstaff and the justice's promise of the new reign.
narrative_structure: A chronicle of endings — of rebellion, of reign, of friendship — built on scenes of age, disease, and memory, with the Gloucestershire justices and the tavern as the comic underworld.
principal_characters: Prince Hal; Sir John Falstaff; King Henry IV; the Lord Chief Justice; Prince John of Lancaster; the Earl of Northumberland; the Archbishop of York; Justice Shallow; Justice Silence; Pistol; Doll Tearsheet; Mistress Quickly; Bardolph; Poins; Lady Percy
meter_and_prosody: Prose dominates the Falstaff scenes and verse the court; the play's elegiac music belongs to its age and sickness.
historical_context: Written about 1597–98; its Epilogue promises the further adventures of Falstaff, fulfilled instead in The Merry Wives of Windsor.
literary_significance: The most sombre of the histories — a study of the costs of power whose rejection scene is among the most painful in the canon.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1600; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Henry V
alternative_titles: The Life of Henry the Fifth
description: The climax of the second tetralogy: the Chorus's apology for the 'wooden O' frames the epic of Agincourt — Henry's claim to France, the traitors at Southampton, Harfleur's breach, the night before battle, and the victory of the 'band of brothers' — followed by the comic peace of the wooing of Katherine.
plot_or_argument: Henry, urged by the church and provoked by the Dauphin's tennis balls, invades France; the campaign moves through Harfleur to Agincourt, where the outnumbered English win; the play closes with the treaty of Troyes and the king's rough wooing of the French princess.
narrative_structure: A choric five-act epic, each act introduced by the Chorus, alternating the high rhetoric of war with the low comedy of the tavern remnants (Bardolph, Pistol, Fluellen) and ending in the romance of the wooing scene.
principal_characters: King Henry V; the Chorus; the Duke of Exeter; Fluellen; Pistol; Bardolph; Nym; Mistress Quickly; the Dauphin; the Constable of France; Katherine; Princess of France; Alice; Montjoy; Williams; the King of France
meter_and_prosody: The great set speeches — 'Once more unto the breach', the Crispin's Day oration — in verse, against the prose of the soldiers and the dialect comedy of the captains.
historical_context: Written 1599, the year of the Globe and of Essex's Irish expedition (to which the Chorus looks forward); the play made Agincourt the founding myth of English arms.
literary_significance: The national epic of the English stage — and, in its ambivalences, the most debated of the histories in every age of war.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1600; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Henry VIII
alternative_titles: The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eighth
description: The last of the history plays, written with John Fletcher: the pageant-like fall of Buckingham, the trial and divorce of Katherine of Aragon, the rise of Anne Bullen and of Cranmer, and the christening of the infant Elizabeth — ending in Cranmer's prophecy of the golden age to come under the 'maiden phoenix'.
plot_or_argument: Buckingham falls to Wolsey's faction; the king's conscience turns against his marriage; Katherine defends herself at the legatine trial; Wolsey's fall follows; Anne is crowned and Elizabeth christened, with Cranmer's prophetic blessing on the new reign.
narrative_structure: A series of state show-scenes — trials, coronations, christenings — in the masque-like mode of late Jacobean spectacle, structured as successive falls and risings.
principal_characters: King Henry VIII; Cardinal Wolsey; Queen Katherine of Aragon; Anne Bullen; the Duke of Buckingham; Thomas Cranmer; the Duke of Norfolk; the Duke of Suffolk; Gardiner; Cromwell; the Old Lady
meter_and_prosody: Verse of late-Shakespearean looseness with Fletcherian run-on lines; the trial scene of Katherine is its moral and poetic summit.
historical_context: First performed 29 June 1613 at the Globe, when the firing of the chambers set the theatre alight and burned it down — the play's alternate title, All Is True, is the one recorded at that performance.
literary_significance: The Stuart court's official version of the Reformation, and the last flowering of the history play Shakespeare had invented.
attribution_notes: Collaboration with John Fletcher established by stylistic and metrical evidence; the Folio assigns the play to Shakespeare alone.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).
